assessment.nobel_worthiness: The cavity method and message passing turned random constraint-satisfaction problems (random k-SAT, coloring) into solvable statistical-mechanics models with clustering and condensation transitions in solution space. It is a clean, universal mechanism with lasting reach into computer science, inference and learning, which is the kind of idea I trust most.
assessment.attribution: Mézard, Parisi and Virasoro developed the cavity method for spin glasses; Mézard and Zecchina with Parisi applied it to K-satisfiability and survey propagation. Parisi already shared the 2021 prize for disordered systems, so a Mézard-Zecchina award would need a clear argument that the computational and algorithmic extension is a separate discovery. The two credited names support a fair two-person configuration.
assessment.maturity: Roughly 20 years of confirmation by rigorous mathematics (satisfiability threshold proofs, Ding-Sly-Sun) and by use in error-correcting codes and inference. Recognition is timely and the interpretation is stable.
uncertainties: Overlap with the scope of the 2021 prize may weigh against it.
The unlisted contributions of Parisi, Krzakala, Montanari and others to the broader programme are not covered by the credited names.
I rely on memory for the details of the rigorous confirmations.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The KTHNY theory of two-dimensional melting by dissociation of dislocations and then disclinations predicted the hexatic phase, a new state with quasi-long-range orientational order. It is a model case of a simple topological-defect mechanism explaining a messy phase transition, with decisive experimental tests in colloids, liquid crystals and simulations.
assessment.attribution: Halperin and Nelson, and independently Young, produced the dislocation-mediated melting theory, building on Kosterlitz and Thouless. The three credited names form a natural trio, and the 2016 prize recognised Kosterlitz and Thouless for the underlying defect-mediated transitions, so it is a delicate question whether the follow-on is distinct enough for a separate prize.
assessment.maturity: The theory dates from 1978-79 and has had decades of experimental and numerical confirmation, including a debated first-order versus continuous melting scenario that has been resolved only recently in colloidal and hard-disk systems. It is mature and arguably late.
uncertainties: The 2016 prize partly covered related ground, which raises a precedent question.
The universality of melting in different 2D systems (first-order versus continuous) has been disputed.
Halperin's name also appears on another candidate, which could matter for the allocation across candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Liquid-liquid phase separation as a principle of intracellular organisation (P granules, nucleoli, condensates) brings concepts from soft-matter statistical physics, such as droplets, surface tension and active chemical reactions, into cell biology. The discovery is original and its reach in biology is large. Whether it is a physics prize is the main question for the committee.
assessment.attribution: Brangwynne and Hyman made the 2009 P-granule observation and the follow-up work. Jülicher supplied the active-droplet theory. This is a coherent trio, but there is a risk that others (for example Rosen, Rosen-Brangwynne-Hyman lineage, Pappu, Cates in active-matter theory) are viewed as equally decisive; the credited names exclude them.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many independent labs over 15 years. However, the physiological significance and the boundary between true phase separation and other assemblies are still debated, so the interpretation is not fully stable.
uncertainties: It is unclear whether the committee regards this as physics rather than biology or chemistry.
Debates about which condensates are genuine phase-separated liquids and their functional role are unresolved.
Credit is distributed over many contributors beyond the three credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and Berry's geometric phase show that gauge potentials and geometry have physical consequences in quantum mechanics. Both are conceptually simple and general and they underlie topological band theory, polarisation, the quantum Hall effect and holonomic control. Impact is far-reaching and foundational.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov and Bohm (1959) gave the effect, with the earlier Ehrenberg-Siday result; David Bohm is deceased and not credited. Berry (1984) is the clear originator of the geometric phase, with Pancharatnam and Longuet-Higgins as precursors and Simon for the holonomy interpretation. A two-person award for two different discoveries is awkward but possible. Priority questions are exactly the type I would press.
assessment.maturity: Aharonov-Bohm was verified by Chambers (1960) and decisively by Tonomura (1986); Berry phase was measured soon after in optics and NMR. Both are very mature and the recognition is late.
uncertainties: The pairing of two separate discoveries and the omission of Bohm, Ehrenberg and Siday, and Pancharatnam complicate a clean prize.
I rely on memory for the precise priority history.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory is exact in infinite dimensions and became the standard framework for strongly correlated materials, capturing the Mott transition and combining with first-principles methods. It is a clean, controlled approximation that has changed how correlated electrons are computed.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt introduced the infinite-dimension limit (1989), Georges and Kotliar (1992) and Jarrell mapped it onto an impurity problem, and Müller-Hartmann also contributed. The credited names omit Metzner, Jarrell, Rozenberg and Müller-Hartmann (deceased), so a clear and fair trio is difficult.
assessment.maturity: Over 30 years of use and validation, including against cold-atom experiments and cluster extensions. Recognition is mature and arguably overdue, but its status as a discovery versus a method is an open question.
uncertainties: Whether a theoretical method rather than a physical discovery fits the prize criteria.
Contested attribution among Metzner, Vollhardt, Georges, Kotliar and Jarrell.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Time-reversal-invariant topological insulators with a Z2 invariant and protected edge or surface states opened a major field of topological matter. The mechanism is simple and general, and experimental realisation in HgTe followed quickly. Impact on materials and ideas is very large.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele proposed the Z2 quantum spin Hall insulator, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted it in HgTe, and Molenkamp's group observed it; Fu, Kane and Mele and Moore-Balents, with Hsieh and Hasan, extended it to 3D. The credited names for this entry omit Bernevig and Zhang; Zhang is deceased. Choosing Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is plausible but does not resolve the HgTe prediction credit.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed in many materials by independent groups since 2007. The field is mature, although application impact is still limited. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Allocation between Kane, Mele, Hasan, Molenkamp, Bernevig and Zhang is unresolved.
Hasan's 3D experimental contributions would be excluded from my proposed trio.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The BEC-BCS crossover realised with strongly interacting Fermi gases through Feshbach resonances provides a tunable model of fermionic superfluidity with universal thermodynamics (unitary Fermi gas). It links superconductivity, nuclear matter and cold atoms through a universal, simply stated problem.
assessment.attribution: Experimental credit is spread over Jin (deceased), Grimm, Ketterle, Salomon, Thomas, Zwierlein and others; the credited names reflect a plausible subset and omit Ketterle and Zwierlein, who may be seen as decisive. Fair allocation is difficult.
assessment.maturity: Well established since 2002-2005 and replicated, with later precision tests of the equation of state. Ketterle's earlier Nobel in 2001 for BEC partly overlaps the field.
uncertainties: Death of Deborah Jin and omission of Ketterle and Zwierlein complicate attribution.
Earlier cold-atom prizes may reduce appetite for another from this field.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Pulsar-timing-array evidence for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background (2023) opens a new window on the gravitational-wave spectrum, probably from supermassive black-hole binaries. The result is important and novel, with a clean Hellings-Downs correlation signature.
assessment.attribution: The result comes from several collaborations (NANOGrav, EPTA, PPTA, CPTA, IPTA), and the three credited names represent leaders of different arrays but do not capture the full group. Allocation among collaborations is a serious issue.
assessment.maturity: The evidence is at about 3-4 sigma, with the source (binaries versus new physics) still unresolved and no individual-source detection. Premature relative to the other candidates.
uncertainties: The significance is below discovery level and the origin of the signal is not established.
Credit is spread across large collaborations, so a three-person prize is problematic.
